title: The bride's gift
hook: the mahr belongs to the bride

segments.voice: Yesterday, the nikah: offer, acceptance and the consent of both. Your line: a contract of mercy.

A man stands up in the mosque in Medina. A woman has come to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and this man asks to marry her. The Prophet asks him: what do you have to give her? Nothing, he says, only this cloth I'm wearing. If you give her that, the Prophet says, you'll be sitting there with nothing on. Go and look for something, even an iron ring. The man goes. He comes back. Not even an iron ring. The story, in Sahih al-Bukhari, isn't over. But notice what's being searched for, so hard: something for her. Today's word: mahr.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU HAVE TO GIVE HER?` → `ONLY THIS CLOTH.` → `EVEN AN IRON RING.`

segments.voice: Mahr is the bride's gift, given by the groom, and it's part of yesterday's nikah. Surah four, verse four, names it, in Pickthall's translation: "And give unto the women (whom ye marry) free gift of their marriage portions." A free gift. Not a price paid for a person, not a fee to her family. Whose is it? In Islamic law the mahr belongs to the bride. Not to her father, not to her brothers, not to a shared account. Hers. The same verse says that if she chooses, of her own accord, to give some of it back, that's her call. And a little further on, the Qur'an tells husbands not to take back what they gave, even if it was a great amount. Now the story from the hook. The man came back without even a ring. So the Prophet asked: what do you know of the Qur'an? The man named some surahs he knew by heart, and the Prophet married them for what he knew of the Qur'an. Some versions say he was to teach them to her. The gift doesn't have to be gold. It does have to be hers. Today, some couples agree a mahr paid at the wedding, some write part of it into the contract to be paid later, and the schools differ on details like whether there's a minimum. This week ran from schools to law in life: other schools, one row, why they differ, the fatwa, the judge, the nikah, and now the gift. By its end, the questions had turned into who owes what to whom.
screen: `A FREE GIFT, NOT A PRICE.` · `HERS, NOT HER FAMILY'S.` · `WHAT DO YOU KNOW OF THE QUR'AN?` · `PAID NOW, OR WRITTEN IN FOR LATER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you love, and something you could give them that would be wholly theirs, not secretly for you: money, time, or something you know and could teach them. Hold that gift, and notice how it feels to give without keeping a share. If you pray, you can remember that person kindly in your own words.
Mahr. The bride's gift, given by the groom as part of the marriage. The Qur'an calls it a free gift, and it belongs to her. Today's word.
Your line: hers alone. A free gift, not a price, and never her family's. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In a Muslim marriage the groom gives the bride a mahr agreed in the contract, sometimes paid at the wedding and sometimes partly deferred; it belongs to her, and couples choose amounts from the symbolic to the substantial.

options: No. It's a free gift to the bride, and it belongs to her alone.
Right. The mahr goes to her father, who decides how it's spent.

chat.meaning: The Qur'an calls the mahr a free gift. It belongs to the bride, not her father or brothers; she may give some back only of her own accord.
